summary_html: An intake **screen** is elevated to a formal **investigation/assessment** under state criteria. CAPTA and CFSR establish the federal expectations for screening, timelines, and investigative quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening/investigation conditions for funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review framework

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Smith v. Ark. Dep't of Human Servs.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the ALJ's decision keeping the appellant's name on the Child Maltreatment Central Registry, holding that substantial evidence supported the finding that his physical discipline exceeded the reasonable-and-moderate standard.
key_cases.relevance: It illustrates how an intake escalates into an investigation, a true finding, and a contested registry placement.
key_cases.quote: Between two fairly conflicting views, even if the reviewing court might have made a different choice, the agency's decision must not be displaced.

key_cases.case_name: Ark. Dep't of Human Servs. v. Salcido
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the circuit court and reinstated the agency's dismissal of the registry appeal, holding the alleged offender forfeited his administrative hearing by failing to report the disposition of the related criminal case and had not preserved his due-process arguments before the agency.
key_cases.relevance: It maps the procedural track a report follows once escalated: investigation, true finding, notice, and a time-limited right to an administrative hearing.
key_cases.quote: The fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.

key_cases.case_name: Arkansas Department of Human Services v. A.B.
key_cases.holding: The court reinstated the administrative true finding of child maltreatment, holding that the alleged offender's confrontation and cross-examination rights were not violated because he was given but declined the opportunity to subpoena and cross-examine adverse witnesses, and that substantial evidence supported the finding.
key_cases.relevance: It shows what happens procedurally once a screened report is escalated into a full investigation with a named offender.
key_cases.quote: The Arkansas Child Maltreatment Act acknowledges the rights of confrontation and cross-examination in administrative reviews of agency findings of child maltreatment.

key_cases.case_name: Phillips v. Ark. Dep't of Human Servs. & Minor Child
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the adjudication of dependency-neglect based on physical abuse, holding that the circuit court properly weighed the age and size of the child, the location of the injury and the recurrence of bruising in deciding the discipline was not reasonable or moderate.
key_cases.relevance: It shows escalation from investigation and safety plan to a filed petition when the parent withdrew consent.
key_cases.quote: The focus of an adjudication hearing is on the child, not the parent.

key_cases.case_name: C.C.B. v. Arkansas Department of Health & Human Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the order keeping C.C.B.'s name on the Child Maltreatment Central Registry, holding that a party before an administrative agency is entitled to due process but that housing the administrative law judge and the agency's counsel in the same office does not by itself establish bias, and that the appellant bore and failed to carry the burden of proving the procedure invalid.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Arkansas Supreme Court authority describing the track a screened report follows into a Crimes Against Children Division investigation, a true finding, and a contested administrative hearing before an ALJ.
key_cases.quote: We have held that a party appearing before an administrative agency is entitled to due process in the proceedings.

reporting_details: Arkansas is not a universal-reporting state: Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-402(b) names 43 categories of mandated reporter — ending with any person 18 or older who observes abuse, sexual abuse, or sexual exploitation of a child — and § 12-18-402(a) requires each of them to notify the statewide Child Abuse Hotline immediately; mandated reporters may instead file through the secure portal at mandatedreporter.arkansas.gov, while everyone else calls the hotline. The hotline is answered by a civilian member of the Arkansas State Police Crimes Against Children Division (CACD), who decides whether a report is accepted; an accepted report is sent for investigation to either DCFS or CACD depending on the severity of the concerns reported, and Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-602(a) places the investigation duty on both "[t]he Department of Human Services and the Division of Arkansas State Police."

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours (severe maltreatment, the neglect defined in § 12-18-103(14)(B), or a child's sudden and unexpected death); 72 hours for all other reports
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Initial notification of suspected child maltreatment received
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-602

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days to make the investigative determination; one 15-day extension permitted (60 days maximum)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the child maltreatment report from the Child Abuse Hotline (9 CAR § 40-324(a))
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-616(a)(2): the timing requirement "shall not be considered as a factor to alter the investigative determination in any judicial or administrative proceeding"
